items.stem: Which comparison correctly describes a coal plant and solar panels supplying electricity to a city?

options.text: Both systems burn fuel that forms over millions of years.
Coal is a finite fuel; panels convert incoming solar energy.
Solar panels replenish coal that the power plant burns.
Using sunlight today reduces the sunlight arriving tomorrow.

items.explanation: Coal is nonrenewable on human timescales. Solar panels capture incoming sunlight; they do not consume a stored supply of solar fuel.

items.stem: Freshwater is renewable through the water cycle. Why can a town still have a limited usable supply?

options.text: Renewable freshwater can be used only once before it disappears.
Renewable resources are available in equal amounts everywhere.
Water is nonrenewable whenever a community uses it.
Drought, withdrawals, pollution, and delivery limits can restrict local availability.

items.explanation: Natural renewal does not guarantee enough usable freshwater at a particular place and time.

items.stem: Evidence A reports NYC average water use of 154.89 gallons/person/day in 2000. What does this number describe?

options.text: Total city daily use divided by the city population.
The exact amount every resident used at home each day.
All water used by the whole city in one year.
The number of people served by each gallon of water.

items.explanation: Per capita is a citywide average. It does not mean every individual used the same amount, and city consumption includes uses beyond homes.

items.stem: Evidence A: NYC population was 7,335,650 in 1990 and 8,175,133 in 2010; average use was 194.09 and 127.09 gallons/person/day. Which comparison is accurate?

options.text: Population and average use per person both increased.
Population fell while average use per person increased.
Population increased while average use per person decreased.
Population and average use per person both stayed constant.

items.explanation: The population values increase, while the average daily use per person values decrease.

items.stem: NYC total consumption was 1,423.8 million gallons/day in 1990 and 1,039.0 million gallons/day in 2010. What does this evidence show?

options.text: Total consumption increased by 384.8 million gallons/day.
Total consumption decreased by 384.8 million gallons/day.
Each resident reduced use by 384.8 gallons/day.
Water quality improved by 384.8 million gallons/day.

items.explanation: Subtracting 1,039.0 from 1,423.8 gives a decrease of 384.8 million gallons/day in total use. The quantity is not per-person use or water quality.

items.stem: Why is population growth alone insufficient to predict a town’s total daily water use?

options.text: Total use depends on both population and average use per person.
Average use per person must rise whenever population rises.
Population has no connection to the amount of water used.
A renewable water supply makes total daily use constant.

items.explanation: People × gallons/person/day = gallons/day. A sufficiently large decrease in average use can offset an increase in population.

items.stem: DEP reported approximately 90 million gallons/day in savings from the 1994–1997 program replacing approximately 1.3 million toilets. How could replacement technology reduce demand?

options.text: It increases the rainfall reaching the water-supply system.
It removes the need for freshwater in all city buildings.
It reduces population by serving fewer city residents.
It provides flushing with less water, lowering water needed for the service.

items.explanation: More efficient fixtures can provide sanitation with less water per flush. The program figure is a DEP-reported approximate savings estimate.

items.stem: A student says NYC’s 1994–1997 Toilet Rebate Program caused the entire 1990–2010 decline in water use. What is the main problem with this claim?

options.text: The program happened outside the 1990–2010 period.
The data measure only toilet use in individual homes.
Other conservation and system-management changes also occurred.
DEP reported no water savings from replacing toilets.

items.explanation: Evidence C supports an approximate program savings figure, not attributing the entire citywide historical decline to one intervention.

items.stem: What additional evidence would be needed to test whether NYC water quality improved while water demand fell?

options.text: Comparable water-quality measurements over time.
Only the number of toilets replaced by the program.
Only the per-person water consumption in 2010.
Only the difference between the two population totals.

items.explanation: Water consumption measures demand. A water-quality claim requires water-quality evidence; lower demand alone does not establish it.

items.stem: A town argues water-efficient fixtures could mitigate pressure on freshwater supplies while serving more people. Which evidence is most relevant?

options.text: NYC’s population totals alone, without any water-use measurements.
NYC’s population and consumption trends plus DEP’s reported replacement-program savings.
NYC rainfall patterns and reservoir capacities, without fixture-use measurements.
The program’s dates and fixture count, without its savings finding or consumption trends.

items.explanation: The historical trends relate population to demand, and the program finding supports a technology mechanism. Neither establishes the town’s exact future savings.
